adapter.reason: Translate two signed coordinate representations and reconcile areas at a kink, rather than simply differentiate a straight line

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select a piecewise signed-slope model; rule selection is explicit rather than hidden

representation_translation.evidence: Translate three x-time segments to two signed frame velocities and area ledgers

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Reconcile intervals, two frame directions, total distance and the corner counterexample

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Only small integer slopes and simple linear coordinate reversal

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Zero-displacement and corner-derivative traps must both be rejected

challenge.prediction: A position–time line changes slope at a sharp corner. Can its instantaneous velocity at that exact instant be read as a single value? Predict before computing.
challenge.prompt: An east-positive rail record is piecewise linear through (t seconds, x metres): (0,1), (2,9), (5,3), (7,3). Observer B uses the reversed coordinate y=15−x. Reconstruct velocities on all intervals in each frame, the signed displacement and path distance of the object, and the signed area check. Decide whether x=3 m at the end means that the cart was always stopped, and whether a unique two-sided instantaneous velocity exists exactly at t=2 s.
challenge.boundaryPrompt: Suppose only the final position becomes x(7)=1 m, while all earlier points and piecewise-linearity remain. What is the last-interval velocity, whole-trip displacement and distance? Record your attempt before revealing the model.
challenge.transfer_difference: Multiple signed segments, a reversed coordinate system, a corner and a counterexample to zero-displacement inference; not a numeric clone of any one worked example.

units.title: Newton's third law from inverse force evidence

adapter.reason: Reconcile two separately measured accelerations and infer interaction-force consistency before testing system-level conservation

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select two distinct recipient FBDs and third-law force pairing

representation_translation.evidence: Translate two sensor accelerations into signed body equations

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Solve contact magnitude independently twice, then check the system centre of mass

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Internal-force cancellation on wrong body is a common exception

challenge.prediction: Can two different measured cart accelerations both agree with equal-and-opposite contact forces? Predict how to check them independently.
challenge.prompt: Two carts A (3 kg) and B (2 kg) are momentarily in horizontal contact on a smooth track. A receives 18 N east from a motor, and B receives 4 N west from a brake. Sensors at one instant report a_A=+2 m/s² and a_B=+4 m/s². Treat east as positive. Independently infer the contact-force magnitude from EACH sensor's body equation, identify the two recipients, and check the centre-of-mass acceleration using both external forces and mass-weighted accelerations. Do these measured accelerations obey Newton's third law?
challenge.boundaryPrompt: If the B sensor instead reported a_B=+3 m/s² while A's report and motor were unchanged, what brake magnitude would restore consistency, assuming the same 12 N contact at that instant?
challenge.transfer_difference: Inverse inference from two independent accelerometers and a system-level consistency test, rather than forward acceleration calculation alone.

adapter.reason: Distinguish equilibrium, driven steady state and phase change under controlled energy-flow evidence and heat capacity

concept_model_selection.evidence: Select a driven steady-state rate model rather than equilibrium or phase-change model

representation_translation.evidence: Translate energy-flow arrows and heat capacities to instantaneous temperature rates

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Connect before/after switching, two systems and a phase-change boundary

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Two simple power divided by heat-capacity calculations

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Constant temperature does not prove equilibrium; phase change invalidates C shortcut

challenge.prediction: If two hot plates have the same measured temperature immediately before switching off their heaters, must they cool at the same initial rate? State why or why not.
challenge.prompt: Two solid plates P and Q, with no phase changes, are held at the same steady temperature above the same room. Just before their heaters switch off, P receives and loses 30 W, while Q receives and loses 40 W. Their effective heat capacities are C_P=200 J/K and C_Q=400 J/K. Immediately after simultaneous switch-off, assume the loss rates are initially unchanged. Classify their original states as equilibrium or driven steady state, infer their initial dU/dt and dT/dt after switch-off, and decide which begins cooling faster. Explain why equal temperature alone did not determine the answer.
challenge.boundaryPrompt: If Q instead contains a phase-changing mixture at constant measured temperature while it loses 40 W after switch-off, can you still use the given effective C_Q to assert −0.10 K/s? What can be inferred from conservation?
challenge.transfer_difference: Combines rate balance, comparative cooling under unequal capacities and phase-boundary falsification, rather than merely identifying one steady plate.

adapter.reason: Choose two distinct geometric path models, reconcile direct and reflected arrival times and test detector resolution

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Compute direct and reflected lengths, then subtract arrival times

algebra_computational_load.evidence: Square-root lengths and unit conversion to milliseconds

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Differential arrival is not elapsed time since emission

challenge.prediction: When source and receiver are different distances from the same wall, does vt/2 applied to the excess delay determine either wall distance? Predict before calculating.
challenge.prompt: On the same side of a large plane wall, a stationary source is 3 m from it and a microphone is 7 m from it; their separation parallel to the wall is 12 m. Assume v=340 m/s and a detector resolves two arrivals only if they differ by at least 10 ms. Calculate direct and reflected path lengths and their times since emission, calculate the excess delay, decide if the detector resolves two separate pulses, and explain precisely why using half of v times the excess delay would be wrong.
challenge.boundaryPrompt: If the microphone were moved to 3 m from the wall while keeping the parallel separation 12 m, what new excess delay would occur at 340 m/s? Does the detector resolve two arrivals?
challenge.transfer_difference: Unequal wall distances, two emission-referenced times and detector resolution with a changed microphone position; distinct from a one-wall symmetric shortcut.
